extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political philosophy and history of political thought (readers of Montesquieu/Rousseau/Voltaire commentary)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and assessing normative and classificatory criteria used to analyze forms of government (Montesquieu and his critics): how governments are defined, classified, and judged according to structure, principles, institutions, and social conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: L'esprit des lois — lois dans leurs rapports avec les circonstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Study laws in relation to all the circumstances that modify them (government, climate, way of life — farmers/hunters/pastoralists — political liberty, religion, commerce, manners, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu's 'esprit des lois' requires that legal/political analysis account for environmental, social, economic and cultural contexts; examples given include government form, climate and manners as causes that shape laws. Anti-pattern: treating laws as abstract, context-free rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by number of governors and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide governments first by number of rulers (one, several, the many) and then by whether they govern for the public good or for the rulers' private interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rulers exercise authority for the general interest the constitution is 'good' (royalty/monarchy, aristocracy, republic); when they govern for their own interest the forms devolve into tyranny, oligarchy, demagogy. Use both count-of-governors and purpose to evaluate legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: nature of government vs principle of government
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature = what makes the government be (its particular structure); principle = what makes it act (the human passions that move it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction is 'very important' and serves as a key for deriving many laws; analyses should separate structural features from motivating social/psychological forces. Examples: structure = 'one, few, many'; principle = 'honor' for monarchy, 'virtue' for republic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereignty as general will (Rousseau) / 'La volonté du souverain est le souverain lui-même'
rubrics_metrics.description: For Rousseau, the sovereign's will is the sovereign; sovereignty resides in the general will — the people as legislator in aggregate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supplies a criterion for democratic legitimacy in which collective will (not particular factions) constitutes sovereign authority. Use caution: commentary notes tension between Rousseau's direct-democracy idea and modern representative institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy is not inherently tied to selection by lot
rubrics_metrics.description: The suffrage by lot (selection by sort) is not of the nature of democracy; democracy should be enlightened and aim to select talent, not rely on random equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical critiques (Socrates, Plato) are cited: random selection is inappropriate for skilled offices (architects, musicians). Anti-pattern: defending sort-based selection as democratic essence without regard to competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public vs secret suffrage: protecting voter freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu's claim that votes must be public is contested; in modern democracies secret ballots have grown because publicity can destroy freedom where many depend on a few.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between elections (where secret voting protects independence) and parliamentary representative votes (where transparency to constituents is generally desirable). Use context to decide which ballot method upholds freedom and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: People-as-lawmakers: limits of the dictum 'the people alone make laws'
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu's maxim that 'the people alone make laws' refers to ancient direct democracies and is contestable in light of representative government and bicameral legislatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat the principle as absolute; modern democracy permits transmission of legislative power to representative assemblies (both lower house and senate). Evaluate claims about 'people making laws' with attention to institutional form (direct vs representative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate powers as a necessary feature of monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: In monarchies the presence of intermediate powers (parliaments, nobility, clergy, municipal bodies) forms the 'nature of the government' and helps contain royal power; their removal leads to despotism or popular state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess monarchy's health by existence and strength of intermediate institutions; historical example: French monarchy weakened by destroying intermediaries, paving way to revolution. Anti-pattern: centralized monarchy lacking buffers tends toward arbitrary rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy vs despotism: abuse vs form
rubrics_metrics.description: Despotism is characterized as an abuse of government, not a distinct form; it can arise in any regime when power is abused — there can be democratic or aristocratic tyrannies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying regimes, differentiate essential form from corrupting abuses; be wary of using 'despotism' as a formal category rather than a label for degenerated rule. Consider civilization/context in interpreting differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation as a principle (especially of aristocracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderation — avoiding excess in power or liberty — is described as the 'soul' of aristocratic government and a virtue that suits reasonable governance generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutions for balance; excessive concentration or excessive license both lead to dysfunction. Note critique that 'moderation' is a vague characteristic and not uniquely aristocratic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as the principle of republics
rubrics_metrics.description: Republics depend on political virtue (love of the state, respect for laws and magistrates, sense of equality); without this virtue republican government collapses into corruption or tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish political (public) virtue from private virtue; civic education and cultural dispositions matter. Anti-pattern: assuming formal institutions alone guarantee republican stability without civic virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education must align with social conditions and begin upon entry to the world
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should be harmonious with the social state into which young people enter; traditional scholastic education lacked such connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess educational aims by how well they prepare citizens for the civic roles required by their polity. Examples: republics prioritize public-minded education; different regimes inculcate differing virtues (honor, frugality, civic duty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frugality and proscriptions on luxury in republics (Montesquieu's view) — contested
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu links frugality and limits on luxury to the survival of republics; critics argue this view wrongly denies individual rights and misunderstands modern democracies where inequality coexists with liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims about economic regulation for civic ends, weigh historical context and modern economic principles (Smith, Turgot). Anti-pattern: legislating stringent restrictions on private enjoyment in the name of republican virtue without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of emergency concentration of power (dictatorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: A concentrated emergency power can sometimes be necessary in a free country but must be compensated by brevity of duration; modern constitutions generally avoid institutionalizing dictatorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate emergency measures for proportionality and temporality; caution against constitutionalizing long-term extraordinary powers which may provoke abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of honor in monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Honor (demand for preferences and distinctions) operates as the principle that helps sustain monarchy; stripping honor/nobility risks degenerating monarchy into despotism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess monarchical systems by the presence of honorific and mediating institutions (nobility, clergy, municipal privileges). Anti-pattern: elimination of intermediate honors leading to arbitrary rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of communistic or austere institutions to small/primitive societies only
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions like community of goods, proscription of money, isolation from foreigners, and monopolies may be defensible in rudimentary small societies but are incompatible with freedom and civilized development in large modern societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not generalize small-society institutions to large polities; evaluate institutional proposals against the size, complexity, and economic needs of the society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music/gymnastics and cultural education as instruments for civic character
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical view (Plato) that cultural forms (music, gymnastics) shape the soul and body, cultivating qualities (courage, restraint) necessary for citizens and soldiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider cultural education's role in forming civic dispositions; use genre-appropriate pedagogies to foster desired civic virtues (e.g., music for tempering courage, gymnastics for physical readiness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Action and reaction between government principle and laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of government acts on laws, and laws act back on the principle — a mechanical action-and-reaction dynamic affecting institutional behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing laws, anticipate reciprocal effects on political psychology and institutions; laws should be assessed for their capacity to reinforce or distort the regime's principle.
